title: Praise on the festivals
hookLine: the Hallel psalms are sung after the Amidah on festivals and new moons

lines: SOME DAYS, A FEW ARE SKIPPED.
cards: Here's a Hebrew word that has traveled far: hallelujah. It's in hymns, gospel songs, a well-known chorus by Handel, a well-known song by Leonard Cohen. It means praise God, hallelu-Yah.

Take the first half, hallel, praise, and make it the name of a set of psalms. On the festivals, they're sung right after the morning Amidah, often with the whole room joining in. On some days, the room sings all of them.
On others, it deliberately skips a few.

teach.b: Hallel is Psalms 113 through 118, six psalms sung together. Near its start, in the old Jewish translation: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof the LORD'S name is to be praised."

And it includes this line, from Psalm 118: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." It's sung on Sukkot, on Shavuot, at the start of Passover, and on all eight days of Hanukkah.
Then there's half Hallel, where parts of two psalms are left out.

teach.h: NONE ON THE DAYS OF JUDGMENT.
teach.b: That's for the new moon each month, and for the last days of Passover. Why only half on the end of Passover? A later explanation draws on a story from the Talmud.
When the Egyptians were drowning in the sea, the angels wanted to sing, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning, and you want to sing? So on those days, the joy is real but held back.
Even a victory has a cost. And on the Days of Awe, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, there's no Hallel at all.

The Talmud gives the reason as a picture: the King sits on the throne of judgment, with the books of life and death open before him. Is this the moment to sing? So Hallel tracks the mood of the calendar.
Full joy, partial joy, and the days when praise goes quiet out of awe.

how: Hallel (Psalms 113–118) is sung after the morning Amidah on Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret, Shavuot, the first day or days of Passover and Hanukkah; a shortened half Hallel is said on Rosh Chodesh and the last days of Passover, and none is said on Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur.

o: a prayer of mourning said at the graveside
the shofar blasts of Rosh Hashanah morning
Psalms 113 to 118, sung as praise on festivals

p: new moons and the end of Passover
no Hallel: the books are open

s: Hallel is sung on Yom Kippur
on the days of judgment there's no Hallel, out of awe.
Hallel is sung on all eight days of Hanukkah
half Hallel leaves out parts of two psalms
a joy that's real but held back.

games.q: it's the last day of Passover, celebrating the crossing of the sea. how much Hallel is sung?
o: full Hallel, the loudest of the year.
games.why: half Hallel. a later explanation recalls God stopping the angels' song as the Egyptians drowned.

practice: Take one line: this is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. If prayer isn't yours, try: this is the day; I'll be glad in it.
Say it once plainly, then sing it to any tune that comes, a little louder than feels normal, and sit in the quiet after the sound.

wordCard.voice: Hallel. Praise: Psalms 113 to 118, sung in full on joyful days, in part on some, and not at all on the Days of Awe.

orig.note: Hebrew: praise. the first half of hallelujah.

carryVoice: Your line: praise on the holidays. Hallel rises and falls with the calendar. That's day six hundred twenty-six.
